docs.title: Flan: Turbulent Trace Impurity Transport
docs.text: Welcome to Flan's documentation! The code is named after Shawn's dog, Flannery. It does not stand for anything. New users to the code see Getting Started for a high-level introduction to the code.

docs.title: Input Options
docs.text:
Input options are set in your input file through the inpts map, e.g.:

inpts["case_name"] = "my_case";
inpts["imp_num"] = 10000;
inpts["imp_mass_amu"] = 183.84;

Any option you don't set uses the default value listed below. The options are grouped by what they control.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text: Option Type Default Description case_name string "undefined" Name of the simulation case. The results are saved to <case_name>.nc. use_gpu string "off" Whether to run the simulation on GPUs. Valid values: "off", "cuda". seed int 4 Base seed for the random number generators. A negative value seeds them from the clock so each run is different. The MPI rank is added to the seed so each rank gets a different sequence. slot_cap int 1048576 Maximum number of particle slots, i.e., the most particles followed at once. The number of slots used is the smaller of this and imp_num. print_interval int 10 Number of progress updates printed while particles are followed. For example, 10 prints an update every 10% of particles.

docs.title: Background plasma
docs.text: Option Type Default Description bkg_source string "gkeyll" Source of the background plasma, either a built-in test background or a Gkeyll simulation. Valid values: "test", "gkeyll". min_ne float 1e15 Lower limit on the electron density (m^-3). min_te float 0.1 Lower limit on the electron temperature (eV). min_ti float 0.1 Lower limit on the ion temperature (eV), applied when calculating collisions with the background ions.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Option Type Default Description test_opt string "gyrate" Which built-in test case to run when using the test background. Valid values: "gyrate", "exb", "gradb", "polarization", "curvature", "friction_force". save_track string "off" Whether to save particle tracks to the output file. Valid values: "off", "on".

docs.title: Gkeyll
docs.text: Option Type Default Description gkyl_dir string "undefined" Directory containing the Gkeyll simulation files. gkyl_casename string "undefined" Name of the Gkeyll case, i.e., the prefix of its output files. gkyl_frame_start int 0 First Gkeyll frame to load. gkyl_frame_end int 1 Last Gkeyll frame to load. The range from gkyl_frame_start to gkyl_frame_end is inclusive. gkyl_elec_name string "elc" Name of the electron species in the Gkeyll simulation. gkyl_ion_name string "ion" Name of the main ion species in the Gkeyll simulation. gkyl_elec_mass_amu float 0.000548 Electron mass used in the Gkeyll simulation (amu). gkyl_ion_mass_amu float 2.014 Main ion mass used in the Gkeyll simulation (amu). gkyl_file_type string "binary" File format of the Gkeyll output. Valid values: "binary". gkyl_moment_type string "bimaxwellian" Type of moment files in the Gkeyll output. Collisions need "bimaxwellian", which provides the ion parallel flow and perpendicular velocity used to calculate the background flow. Valid values: "bimaxwellian", "maxwellian", "m0m1m2". calc_grad_elec string "off" Whether to calculate the electric field gradient. This is not implemented yet, so turning it on only prints a warning. Valid values: "off", "on".

docs.title: Geometry and boundaries
docs.text: Option Type Default Description tbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the start and end of the background time range. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic". min_xbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum x boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_xbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum x boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". min_ybound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum y boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_ybound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum y boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". min_zbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum z boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_zbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum z boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". lcfs_x float 0.0 x coordinate of the last closed flux surface. lcfs_y float 0.0 y coordinate of the last closed flux surface. lcfs_z float 0.0 z coordinate of the last closed flux surface. imp_xbound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the x boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. imp_ybound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the y boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. imp_zbound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the z boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. sep_x_bc_xp_z1 float 0.0 First z value for the separatrix x boundary condition near the X-point. sep_x_bc_xp_z2 float 0.0 Second z value for the separatrix x boundary condition near the X-point.

docs.title: Impurity properties
docs.text: Option Type Default Description imp_atom_num int 74 Atomic number of the impurity. imp_mass_amu float 183.84 Mass of the impurity (amu). imp_init_charge int 1 Charge state the impurities start with.

docs.title: Impurity transport
docs.text: Option Type Default Description imp_num int 1 Total number of impurity particles to follow. imp_tstart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting time is chosen: a single value (imp_tstart_val), uniformly between imp_trange_min and imp_trange_max, or uniformly over the full background time range. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_tstart_val float 0.0 Starting time of every impurity when imp_tstart_opt is "single_value" (s). imp_trange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting time range when imp_tstart_opt is "range" (s). imp_trange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting time range when imp_tstart_opt is "range" (s). imp_xstart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting x coordinate is chosen: a single value (imp_xstart_val), uniformly between imp_xrange_min and imp_xrange_max, or uniformly over the full x range of the background. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_xstart_val float 0.0 Starting x coordinate of every impurity when imp_xstart_opt is "single_value". imp_xrange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting x range when imp_xstart_opt is "range". imp_xrange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting x range when imp_xstart_opt is "range". imp_ystart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting y coordinate is chosen: a single value (imp_ystart_val), uniformly between imp_yrange_min and imp_yrange_max, or uniformly over the full y range of the background. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_ystart_val float 0.0 Starting y coordinate of every impurity when imp_ystart_opt is "single_value". imp_yrange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting y range when imp_ystart_opt is "range". imp_yrange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting y range when imp_ystart_opt is "range". imp_zstart_opt string "single_value" How each impurity's starting z coordinate is chosen: a single value (imp_zstart_val), uniformly between imp_zrange_min and imp_zrange_max, or uniformly over the full z range of the background. Valid values: "single_value", "range", "full_range". imp_zstart_val float 0.0 Starting z coordinate of every impurity when imp_zstart_opt is "single_value". imp_zrange_min float 0.0 Lower limit of the starting z range when imp_zstart_opt is "range". imp_zrange_max float 0.0 Upper limit of the starting z range when imp_zstart_opt is "range". imp_temp_start_opt string "main_ion" How each impurity's starting temperature is chosen: a single value (imp_temp_start_val) or the local main ion temperature. Starting velocities are sampled from an isotropic Maxwellian at this temperature. Valid values: "single_value", "main_ion". imp_temp_start_val float 0.0 Starting temperature of every impurity when imp_temp_start_opt is "single_value" (eV). imp_collisions string "nanbu" Collision model for the impurities, either off or the Nanbu model. Valid values: "off", "nanbu". imp_time_step_opt string "constant" Whether the impurity time step is constant or variable. Valid values: "constant", "variable". imp_time_step float 1e-8 Impurity time step (s). imp_time_step_min float 1e-12 Minimum impurity time step when the time step is variable (s). imp_source_scale_fact float 1.0 Impurity source scaling factor (particles/s), i.e., how many real particles a single simulated particle represents. Used to convert the Monte Carlo counts into a density. imp_iz_recomb string "on" Whether impurity ionization and recombination are on. Valid values: "off", "on". imp_max_time float 1e10 Maximum time a particle is followed for (s). A particle that exceeds it is killed and counted in a warning at the end of the run.

docs.title: Variance reduction (temporarily removed)
docs.text: Option Type Default Description var_red_split string "off" When particles are split for variance reduction: never, at ionization/recombination events, or at collisions. Valid values: "off", "iz_rec", "coll". var_red_import string "median" Method used to calculate particle importance for variance reduction. Valid values: "median", "exp_dist", "exp_time". var_red_freq float 0.1 How often variance reduction is applied. var_red_min_weight float 0.1 Minimum particle weight for variance reduction. var_red_med_mod float 1.0 Modifier applied to the median importance for variance reduction. var_red_rusrol string "off" Whether to use Russian roulette for variance reduction. Valid values: "off", "on". var_red_rusrol_prob float 0.5 Probability used for Russian roulette.

docs.title: OpenADAS
docs.text: Option Type Default Description openadas_root string "undefined" Directory containing the OpenADAS rate coefficient files. openadas_year int 50 Year of the OpenADAS data files to use.

docs.title: Journal Articles
docs.text:
• S. A. Zamperini, T. N. Bernard, S. Andersen, A. C. D. Hoffmann, D. L. Rudakov, and T. Abrams, "Fully generalized, turbulent trace impurity transport with Gkeyll and Flan in the DIII-D far-SOL," Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion 68, 075013 (2026). doi:10.1088/1361-6587/ae836b

    The first official Flan publication. Validation tests are shown, and tungsten transport in the DIII-D far-SOL is simulated. Main takeaways are an early attempt at extracting the anomalous diffusion and pinch velocities as well as the observation that transport away from the wall increases with atomic number.

  • S. A. Zamperini, T. N. Bernard, D. L. Rudakov, and J. A. Boedo, "Turbulent drifts of impurity ions as an explanation for anomalous radial transport in the far-SOL of DIII-D," Nuclear Fusion 64, 074002 (2024). doi:10.1088/1741-4326/ad4c78

    A python-based precursor to Flan that tracked impurities via their guiding centers. It became clear that the guiding center approximation was violated because the fluctuations were on the same scale as the tungsten gyroradius, and that the full gyro-orbit needed to be resolved. This was the key issue that showed the need for a proper high-performance code that resolved the gyro-orbit and all the additional Monte Carlo structure.

docs.title: Linux Installation
docs.text: Installing Flan on a general Linux machine involves downloading and compiling the dependencies and then compiling the code via CMake.

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
Navigate to the top-level flan/ directory and run:

machines/mkdeps.linux.sh

This will download and install all the dependencies in $HOME/flansoft by default. If you wish to have them installed elsewhere, change the following line in mkdeps.linux.sh to the desired directory:

export FLANSOFT=/path/to/dir/flansoft

This script also handles creating the conda environment that Flan must run in. You must activate the environment before running Flan with conda activate flan.

docs.title: Install Flan
docs.text:
Navigate to flan/build. This is where Flan will be compiled as a library. Run CMake to create the Makefile, then make and install the library.

cd build
cmake ..
make && make install

Flan will be installed at flan/lib/libflan.so. This also creates a bash script scripts/flan_setup.sh, which is used when setting up a new case.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: There are probably numerous issues that can pop up, as each machine is different. Please reach out to a developer if you encounter issues so the instructions can be updated.

docs.title: Perlmutter Installation
docs.text: Installing Flan on Perlmutter involves downloading and compiling the dependencies and then compiling the code via CMake. It uses the NERSC provided Cray C/C++ compiler wrappers (cc/CC).

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
Navigate to the top-level flan/ directory and run:

machines/mkdeps.perlmutter.sh

This will download and install all the dependencies in $HOME/flansoft by default. If you wish to have them installed elsewhere, change the following line in mkdeps.perlmutter.sh to the desired directory:

export FLANSOFT=/path/to/dir/flansoft

This script also handles creating the conda environment that Flan must run in. You must activate the environment before running Flan by first loading the conda module with module load conda and then activating the environment with conda activate flan.

docs.title: Install Flan
docs.text:
Navigate to flan/build. This is where Flan will be compiled as a library. Run CMake to create the Makefile, then make and install the library. On Perlmutter you should enable CUDA.

cd build
cmake .. -DENABLE_CUDA=ON
make && make install

Flan will be installed at flan/lib/libflan.so.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Flan is built as a modern C++23 project using CMake and supports both serial and hybrid MPI/OpenMP execution. This page walks you through installing and building Flan on laptops, workstations, and HPC systems such as Perlmutter.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Flan has the following dependencies:

  • C++23-capable compiler
  • CMake ≥ 3.26
  • OpenMP support
  • MPI
  • MPICH, OpenMPI, Cray-MPICH, etc.
  • HDF5
  • NetCDF
  • zlib
  • conda (or mamba)

HDF5, NetCDF and zlib are installed by machine-specific scripts to install dependencies, found in machines/. Other dependencies must be provided by the computing environment.

docs.title: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Cloning the repository is straightforward. This will clone it into flan/:

git clone https://github.com/shawnzamperini/flan.git

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Setting up a Flan case from scratch consists of the following steps:

  • Create case directory: flan_setup.sh
  • Modify input file
  • Compile input file with Flan
  • Run case/submit job

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A built-in test case that demonstrates the ExB drift with a single particle will be used to show how to run Flan. First create the run directory with the command:

/path/to/flan/scripts/flan_setup.sh test_exb

This will create a directory called test_exb and populate it with an empty input file as well as the needed files to compile it with Flan. We will not cover the various input options here, and will instead copy over the input file used to run the ExB drift test:

cd test_exb
cp /path/to/flan/tests/test_exb.cpp .

The input file must have the same name as the directory because it is baked into the Makefile that was generated to compile the input file. Flan must be run in the conda environment that was created as part of the installation process because it contains some needed paths, primarily for interfacing with Gkeyll data. Ensure it's activated with conda activate flan. You typically will see (flan) at the start of your command line when it's activated. Next make the input file with just make.

Running the simulation depends on if you can run it from the command line or need to use a job scheduler. Running from the command line will be covered first, and job submission scripts will be provided after.

docs.title: Running from Command Line
docs.text:
To run from the command line simply run the executable:

./test_exb

By default, this will run with one MPI process and likely the maximum number of OpenMP threads available. On smaller machines like laptops or workstations only one MPI processes is needed since it is mainly for distributed computing across multiple compute nodes, such as on clusters. To explicitly set the number of OpenMP threads used by Flan, e.g., to 5, use:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 ./test_exb

You may often need to reduce the number of OpenMP threads to stay within memory limits of your machine, as each thread comes with memory overhead.

To control the number of MPI processes, e.g., to use 2, use:

mpiexec -np 2 ./test_exb

Alternative commands include mpirun and srun, depending on your system.

Control the number of OpenMP threads available to each process the same as before:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 mpiexec -np 2 ./test_exb

docs.title: Perlmutter Batch Script
docs.text:
The following is an example batch script used to submit a Flan job on Perlmutter. 

#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH --job-name=my-job-name
#SBATCH --account=m3739     # Update with project number
#SBATCH --nodes=2           # 2 nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=2          # 2 MPI tasks
#SBATCH --constraint=cpu
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=128 # Use all CPUs on node
#SBATCH --qos=regular       # debug (only one node allowed) or regular
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00     # Run for an hour

# OpenMP settings
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK      # Match --cpus-per-task above
export OMP_PLACES=cores         # Bind threads to cores
export OMP_PROC_BIND=spread     # Spread threads across cores

# This controls the number of threads available in python. Make it match
# cpus-per-task
export NUMEXPR_MAX_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

# Initialize conda for compute node
module load conda
conda activate flan

# Run Flan run
srun --cpu-bind=cores ./my_flan_case
Compile the input file as normal, using the Makefile provided when setting up a case directory. If the batch script is saved as submit-flan-perlmutter.sh, then submit the job with:

sbatch submit-flan-perlmutter.sh

Output is put into a generically named slurm file.

docs.title: function broadcast
docs.text:
void Background::Background::broadcast (
    MPI_Comm comm
)

Broadcasts the background from rank 0 to every other MPI rank.

Every rank must call this. After it returns, every rank holds a copy of the dimensions, the times and computational grid, the geometry data and the plasma and field data loaded on rank 0. Not broadcast are the time and grid min/max values, bR, the covariant magnetic field components (b_x, b_y, b_z) and the electric field gradient (gradeX, gradeY, gradeZ).

Parameters:

  • comm MPI communicator to broadcast over.

docs.title: function check_dim
docs.text:
bool Background::Background::check_dim (
    const int m_dim,
    const int in_dim,
    const std::string_view data,
    const int dim_num
)

Checks that a new dimension matches the dimension already stored.

A stored dimension of 0 means it has not been set yet, so any new dimension is accepted. Otherwise the two must be equal. A mismatch means the data is not being read in correctly or is from different Gkeyll runs, and an error message with both values is printed.

Parameters:

  • m_dim Dimension currently stored in the Background.
  • in_dim Dimension of the data being loaded.
  • data Name of the data being loaded (for the error message).
  • dim_num Which dimension (1-4) is being checked (for the error message).

Returns:

True if the dimensions are consistent, false otherwise.

docs.title: function interp_4d
docs.text:
BkgFPType Background::Background::interp_4d (
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & vec4d,
    const double t0,
    const double x0,
    const double y0,
    const double z0
) const

Interpolates 4D background data at a given time and position.

This is a convenience wrapper around Utilities::interp_vec4d that passes in the background times and the x, y and z cell centers, so callers only need to supply the data and the point to evaluate it at.

Parameters:

  • vec4d Data to interpolate, stored as a function of (t, x, y, z).
  • t0 Time at which to evaluate the data.
  • x0 x-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.
  • y0 y-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.
  • z0 z-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.

Returns:

Interpolated value at (t0, x0, y0, z0).

docs.title: function set_dims
docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Background::Background::set_dims (
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & v,
    const std::string_view data
)

Checks the dimensions of a Vector4D against the stored dimensions and stores them if they are consistent.

Each of the four dimensions of v is checked with check_dim. If all four are consistent, they become the stored dimensions. If any are not, an error message is printed and the stored dimensions are left unchanged. The program is not stopped.

Template parameters:

  • T Data type stored in the Vector4D.

Parameters:

  • v Vector4D whose dimensions are checked.
  • data Name of the data being loaded (for the error message).

    double & bkg_vX,

Samples a velocity from a drifting Maxwellian distribution.

The distribution has temperature T and bulk velocity (uX, uY, uZ).

Parameters:

  • T Temperature [eV].
  • uX Drift velocity x-component [m/s].
  • uY Drift velocity y-component [m/s].
  • uZ Drift velocity z-component [m/s].
  • m Particle mass [kg].
  • rng Random number generator.
  • bkg_vX Sampled x-velocity [m/s].
  • bkg_vY Sampled y-velocity [m/s].
  • bkg_vZ Sampled z-velocity [m/s].

docs.title: function check_tdim
docs.text:
Check that the number of frames in the loaded background matches that requested for the simulation. 

void Gkyl::check_tdim (
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_arr,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

This only need to be run once. It is useful if the user is reusing an already calculated background, but changed the frames in the input file. In that case the background files should be deleted so that they can be regenerated, since the default is to read any existing files. Note you can circumvent this error checking if the range of frames stays the same, but that's fringe case and not worth the effort to protect against at the moment.

docs.title: function read_data_pgkyl
docs.text:
Function to read in Gkeyll data using a python interface to postgkyl via read_gkyl.py. 

template<typename T>
void Gkyl::read_data_pgkyl (
    const std::string & species,
    const std::string & data_type,
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_data,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double species_mass_amu=0,
    const bool force_load=false
)

This produces the following csv files: bkg_from_pgkyl_times.csv : The time for each frame bkg_from_pgkyl_grid.csv : Nodes for grid bkg_from_pgkyl_density.csv : Density arrays for all frames bkg_from_pgkyl_temperature.csv : Temperature arrays for all frames bkg_from_pgkyl_potential.csv : Plasma potential arrays for all frames bkg_from_pgkyl_magnetic_field.csv : Magnetic field arrays for all frames The data is loaded and placed into gkyl_data accordingly.

Parameters:

  • species Name of the species for the Gkeyll run
  • data_type Name of the data to load. Can be one of temperature, density, potential or magnetic field.
  • gkyl_data One of the global (to the Gkyl namespace) vectors that corredponds to the data_type being loaded.
  • opts Options object that contains all the controlling options of the simulation.
  • species_mass_amu The mass of the species in amu.

docs.text:
Calculate impurity density from data stored in counts and weights. 

void Impurity::Statistics::calc_density (
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const int tot_imp_num,
    const double imp_source_scale_fact=1.0
)

Parameters:

  • bkg The Background object used in the simulation
  • tot_imp_num The total number of impurity ions followed (primary and secondary)
  • imp_source_scale_fact A scaling factor related to the impurity source in units of particles/s. Essentially says how many particles a single particle represents.

Calculate the density in each cell using the Monte Carlo counts and weights. The Background is needed to get the cell volumes. As of now, imp_source_scale_fact is user supplied, but it hasn't been fully thought out yet. This only works for uniform Cartesian grids right now, but it can be generalized.

docs.title: function all_dead_wrapper
docs.text:
bool ImpurityTransport::all_dead_wrapper (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    Slots::SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    int rem_parts
)

Checks whether the simulation is finished, choosing the CPU or GPU implementation.

The simulation is finished when no particles are waiting to be launched and every particle in slots is dead. If rem_parts is positive, false is returned without checking slots. If GPU acceleration is on (use_gpu), Slots::all_dead_gpu is called, which copies data from the GPU and so implicitly synchronizes it. The GPU branch only exists in CUDA builds.

Parameters:

  • slots Host-side particle slots (used on the CPU path).
  • slots_d Device-side particle slots (used on the GPU path).
  • opts Simulation options, used to check whether the GPU is on.
  • rem_parts Number of particles still waiting to be launched.

Returns:

True if no particles remain to be launched and every slot is dead, false otherwise.

If GPU acceleration is on (use_gpu), Boris::update_velocity_gpu is called. Otherwise Boris::update_velocity_cpu is called. The GPU branch only exists in CUDA builds. A negative dt pushes the velocities backward in time, which main_loop uses to offset the starting velocities by half a time step.

void ImpurityTransport::collision_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const double dt,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    Impurity::Statistics & imp_stats,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs

Applies Coulomb collisions with the background ions and electrons to every particle in slots (CPU implementation).

Particle velocities are updated in place with the Nanbu collision model. Collisions with the background ions are always applied. Collisions with the electrons are applied afterwards, except for the friction_force test case, which only considers ion collisions so the result can be compared against the expected flow.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots whose velocities are updated.
  • bkg Background plasma that provides the ion and electron properties.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • opts Simulation options, used to check the test_opt option.
  • imp_stats Impurity statistics passed through to the collision model.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread.

docs.title: function find_containing_cell_cpu
docs.text:
void ImpurityTransport::find_containing_cell_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg
)

Finds the background time index and spatial cell indices for every particle in slots (CPU implementation).

Time and space are handled differently. The background times are stored at "time centers" rather than on a grid, so the time index is the index of the background time nearest to the particle's time. The spatial coordinates are defined by grid edges, so each spatial index is the index of the cell that contains the particle's x, y and z coordinates. Particles outside the grid are assigned the first or last cell in that dimension.

The indices are written back into slots with set_tidx, set_xidx, set_yidx and set_zidx. The loop over particles is parallelized with OpenMP. Every slot is updated, including slots holding dead particles.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots whose positions are read and whose time and cell indices are updated.
  • bkg Background plasma that provides the time array and the x, y and z grid edges.

docs.title: function follow_impurities
docs.text:
Impurity::Statistics ImpurityTransport::follow_impurities (
    Background::Background & bkg,
    Options::Options & opts,
    Timer::Timer & timer
)

Follows every impurity particle through the background plasma and returns the accumulated statistics.

This is the top-level driver for impurity transport. It sets up the impurity statistics arrays, loads the OpenADAS rate coefficients (one MPI rank at a time, to avoid every rank reading the same files at once) and allocates the particle slots, with min(slot_cap, imp_num) slots. All slots start dead so the first fill launches particles into them.

On GPUs, the data is copied to each GPU, a random number generator is set up for each GPU thread, and gpu_worker runs main_loop on every GPU concurrently. The statistics and timers from each GPU are then combined and the device memory is freed. On CPUs, one random number generator is created per OpenMP thread and main_loop is called directly. If GPU acceleration was requested in a build without CUDA, it is turned off.

If the seed option is negative, random number generators are seeded from the clock so each run is different. Otherwise the seed option is used. In both cases the MPI rank is added to the seed so each rank gets a different sequence.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma to follow the particles through.
  • opts Simulation options. use_gpu may be turned off if Flan was built without GPU support.
  • timer Timer that accumulates the time spent in each step.

Returns:

Impurity statistics accumulated from every particle followed on this rank.

docs.text:
void ImpurityTransport::main_loop (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    Slots::SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice & bkg_d,
    Impurity::Statistics & imp_stats,
    ImpurityStats::StatisticsDevice & imp_stats_d,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADAS & oa_ioniz,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADASDevice & oa_ioniz_d,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADAS & oa_recomb,
    const OpenADAS::OpenADASDevice & oa_recomb_d,
    Options::Options & opts,
    Options::OptionsDevice * opts_d,
    Timer::Timer & timer,
    int & ioniz_warnings,
    int & recomb_warnings,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs,
    pcg32 * rngs_d,
    int & max_time_ctr
)

Runs the main particle-following loop until every particle has been launched and followed until it dies.

The imp_num particles are split evenly between the MPI ranks, with the remainder going to the last rank. When running on GPUs, each rank's share is split again between its GPUs, with the remainder going to device 0. The slots are then filled, and the starting velocities are pushed back half a time step as the Boris algorithm requires. Each iteration of the loop then:

  • Updates charge states from ionization/recombination (if imp_iz_recomb is on).
  • Applies collisions (if imp_collisions is on).
  • Updates velocities with the Boris algorithm.
  • Advances particle positions.
  • Checks the time and spatial bounds.
  • Replaces dead particles with new ones.
  • Finds the containing cell of each particle.
  • Records statistics.

Each step is timed with a scoped timer. Progress is printed by rank 0 and GPU device 0 only.

Parameters:

  • slots Host-side particle slots.
  • slots_d Device-side particle slots (GPU only).
  • bkg Host-side background plasma.
  • bkg_d Device-side background plasma (GPU only).
  • imp_stats Host-side impurity statistics.
  • imp_stats_d Device-side impurity statistics (GPU only).
  • oa_ioniz Host-side OpenADAS ionization rate coefficients.
  • oa_ioniz_d Device-side OpenADAS ionization rate coefficients (GPU only).
  • oa_recomb Host-side OpenADAS recombination rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb_d Device-side OpenADAS recombination rate coefficients (GPU only).
  • opts Simulation options.
  • opts_d Device-side simulation options (GPU only).
  • timer Timer that accumulates the time spent in each step.
  • ioniz_warnings Counter of particles whose ionization probability exceeded 1.
  • recomb_warnings Counter of particles whose recombination probability exceeded 1.
  • rngs Host-side random number generators, one per OpenMP thread (CPU only).
  • rngs_d Device-side random number generators (GPU only).
  • max_time_ctr Counter of particles that exceeded the maximum allowed time.

docs.title: function step_cpu
docs.text:
void ImpurityTransport::step_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double dt,
    int & max_time_ctr
)

Advances every alive particle in slots by one time step (CPU implementation).

Each alive particle's time since launch (pt) and background time (t) are increased by dt, and its x, y and z positions are advanced using its current velocity. If the particle's time since launch exceeds the imp_max_time option, the particle is marked dead and max_time_ctr is incremented. The iteration counter of each stepped particle is also incremented. Dead particles are skipped. The loop over particles is parallelized with OpenMP.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots to advance.
  • bkg Background plasma (currently unused).
  • opts Simulation options, used for imp_max_time.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • max_time_ctr Counter of particles that exceeded the maximum allowed time. Incremented atomically.

docs.text: Default values for every option are included in the definitions of each member variable. These can then be overwritten as in load_options.cpp

docs.title: function Options
docs.text:
Options::Options::Options ()

Constructs an Options object with every option at its default value.

The defaults are set where each member variable is declared in options.h. The control integers are then set to match the default string options by calling initialize_control_ints.

docs.title: function get_control_int
docs.text:
int Options::Options::get_control_int (
    const std::string & var_name,
    const int control_int
) const

Returns a control integer after checking that it was set.

Control integers start at -1, meaning not set. If control_int is still negative, an error is printed. This usually means the option's setter is missing from initialize_control_ints. The value is returned either way.

Parameters:

  • var_name Name of the option the control integer belongs to (for the error message).
  • control_int Control integer to check.

Returns:

The control integer, unchanged.

docs.title: function initialize_control_ints
docs.text:
void Options::Options::initialize_control_ints ()

Sets every control integer to match its string option.

Control integers are integer versions of string options that are faster to check in the code than comparing strings. The logic that assigns each one lives in the option's setter, so this calls every such setter with the option's current value. Any new option with a control integer must have its setter called here too. Otherwise its control integer stays at -1, which get_control_int reports as an error.

docs.title: function bilinear_interp
docs.text:
template<typename T>
inline T Utilities::bilinear_interp (
    const T *__restrict__ table,
    const T *__restrict__ x_grid,
    int nx,
    const T *__restrict__ y_grid,
    int ny,
    T x,
    T y
)

Performs bilinear interpolation on a flattened two-dimensional lookup table stored in device memory.

The function locates the grid cell that contains the point (x, y), computes the interpolation weights in each dimension, and returns the bilinearly interpolated value. Interpolation weights are clamped to the range [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation beyond the boundaries of the tabulated data.

The table is assumed to be stored in row-major order with dimensions nx × ny, where the flattened index corresponding to (ix, iy) is ix * ny + iy.

Template parameters:

  • T Floating-point data type used for the table and coordinate arrays.

Parameters:

  • table Flattened two-dimensional lookup table of size nx * ny.
  • x_grid Monotonically increasing x-coordinate array of length nx.
  • nx Number of x-grid points.
  • y_grid Monotonically increasing y-coordinate array of length ny.
  • ny Number of y-grid points.
  • x X-coordinate at which to evaluate the table.
  • y Y-coordinate at which to evaluate the table.

Returns:

Bilinearly interpolated value at (x, y).

Performs bilinear interpolation within a rectangular region in two-dimensional (x, y) space.

The function interpolates a value at the coordinates (x, y) using values defined at the corners of a rectangle bounded by (x0, y0) and (x1, y1).

Parameters:

  • x0 Lower x-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • y0 Lower y-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • z0 Value at the lower corner.
  • x1 Upper x-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • y1 Upper y-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • z1 Value at the upper corner.
  • x X-coordinate at which to evaluate the interpolated value.
  • y Y-coordinate at which to evaluate the interpolated value.

Returns:

Bilinearly interpolated value at (x, y). Performs bilinear interpolation within a rectangular region in two-dimensional (x, y) space.

The rectangle is defined by the coordinates (x0, y0) and (x1, y1), with values specified at each of the four corners. Interpolation is performed first along the x direction and then along the y direction to obtain the value at (x, y).

Corner indexing follows the usual convention:

z00 : (x0, y0) z10 : (x1, y0) z01 : (x0, y1) z11 : (x1, y1)

std::pair< int, int > Utilities::bracket_indices (
    const std::vector< double > & x,
    double x0
)

Finds the indices of the two grid points that bracket a specified coordinate value.

For values within the coordinate range, the returned indices correspond to the nearest lower and upper grid points that surround x0. For values outside the coordinate range, the first or last valid interval is returned so that interpolation can proceed without accessing elements beyond the array bounds.

The input coordinate array is assumed to be sorted in ascending order.

Parameters:

  • x Sorted coordinate array.
  • x0 Coordinate value for which bracketing indices are sought.

Returns:

Pair containing the lower and upper bracketing indices {lo, hi}.

docs.text:
template<typename T>
int Utilities::get_neighbor_index (
    const double val,
    const std::vector< T > & cell_centers,
    const int idx
)

Returns the index of the nearest neighboring cell center to a specified cell center index.

The neighbor is selected based on which side of the cell center the value lies. If the value is greater than the cell center, the neighboring index to the right is returned. If the value is less than or equal to the cell center, the neighboring index to the left is returned.

At the edges of the grid, where only one neighboring cell exists, that neighbor is returned regardless of which side of the cell center the value lies on.

Template parameters:

  • T Data type of the cell center coordinates.

Parameters:

  • val Coordinate value of interest.
  • cell_centers Array of cell center coordinates.
  • idx Index of the reference cell center.

Returns:

Index of the neighboring cell center closest to the side of the cell containing val.

Broadcasts a vector from a root MPI rank to all other ranks in the communicator.

The root rank provides the vector contents and size. The vector size is first broadcast to all ranks, allowing non-root ranks to resize their local vectors before the vector data itself is broadcast.

The element type T must have a corresponding MPI datatype defined through mpi_type<T>::type.

Splits a string into whitespace-delimited tokens.

Consecutive whitespace characters are treated as a single delimiter, and leading or trailing whitespace is ignored. The resulting vector contains each extracted token in the order it appears in the input string.

Internally, the string is parsed using a std::istringstream and repeated applications of the stream extraction operator.

Performs trilinear interpolation within a rectangular cell in (x, y, z) space.

The cell is defined by the coordinates (x0, y0, z0) and (x1, y1, z1), with values specified at each of the eight cell corners. Interpolation weights are clamped to the range [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation beyond the cell boundaries. As a result, points outside the cell return the value on the nearest cell face, edge, or corner.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text: This class provides an intuitive interface to 4D data. A value at a particular index is accessed by indexing via the parentheses operator, e.g., vec(i,j,k,l). The underlying data is stored as a contiguous 1D vector.

docs.title: function Vector4D [4/5]
docs.text:
Artificial constructor that should not be directly called. 

Vectors::Vector4D::Vector4D (
    std::vector< T > data_in,
    int dim1,
    int dim2,
    int dim3
)

Artificial constructor to allow us to compile read_gkyl.load_values. That function selectively returns a brace-enclosed initializer list for either a Vector3D or Vector4D based on the template parameter. The compiler nonetheless needs to see a constructor for Vector4D that accepts these inputs, since that is what Vector3D uses. This constructor should never get used.

docs.title: function Vector4D [5/5]
docs.text:
Copy constructor. 

Vectors::Vector4D::Vector4D (
    const Vector4D & v
)

We can make the copy constructor yell at us since we probably never want to make a copy of a Vector4D, with the exception of when a Vector4D is involved in an OpenMP reduction (in that case you need to make a copy for each thread. Useful to uncomment out this print statement to check for inefficiencies.

namespace Indices
{
    // Finding nearest index CUDA. This is the same logic as 
    // get_nearest_index_cpu in indices.h just without STL.
    template <typename T>
    __device__ int get_nearest_index_cuda(const T* vec, int N, T value)
    {
        // Manual lower_bound
        int left = 0;
        int right = N;

        // This is essentially std::lower. Find the index of the first value
        // in vec that is larger than value with a binary search.
        while (left < right)
        {
            int mid = (left + right) >> 1;  // (left + right) / 2
            if (vec[mid] < value)
                left = mid + 1;
            else
                right = mid;
        }

        int index = left;

        // Boundary cases
        if (index == 0)
            return 0;

        if (index == N)
            return N - 1;

        // Compare vec[index] vs vec[index-1]
        T diff_low  = vec[index]   - value;
        T diff_prev = vec[index-1] - value;

        // Absolute value
        if (diff_low < 0)  diff_low  = -diff_low;
        if (diff_prev < 0) diff_prev = -diff_prev;

        // Return the closer index
        return (diff_low < diff_prev) ? index : (index - 1);
    }   


    // Finding nearest cell index from a grid on CUDA. This is the same logic as 
    // get_nearest_cell_index_cpu in indices.h just without STL.
    template <typename T>
    __device__ int get_nearest_cell_index_cuda(const T* grid_edges, int N, 
        T value)
    {
        // This is essentially std::lower. Find the index of the first value
        // in grid_edges that is larger than value with a binary search.
        int left = 0;
        int right = N;
        while (left < right)
        {
            int mid = (left + right) >> 1;  // (left + right) / 2

            if (grid_edges[mid] < value)
                left = mid + 1;
            else
                right = mid;
        }

        int index = left;

        // Realize that one minus the index represented by lower is the value
        // we're after in the vectors with values at the cell centers.
        //  ____________
        //  |_0_|_1_|_2_|  <-- cell center indices
        //  0   1   2   3  <-- grid_edges indices
        //          ^
        //        lower
        //
        // In this example, we want 1 returned, so we return 2 - 1 = 1. If
        // value is outside the range, return the index of the respective end
        // of the vector.

        // If value is less than everything return the first cell
        if (index == 0)
            return 0;

        // If value is larger than everything return the last cell
        else if (index == N)
            return N - 2;
        else
            return index - 1;
    }

}  // namespace Indices

#pragma once
#include <cstdio>

#include "background_device.h"

#include "device_constants.cuh"
#include "interpolate.cuh"
#include "utilities.cuh"


namespace Interpolate
{

    // A stencil to hold the indices of cells surrounding a point that we
    // wish to interpolate at. We reuse this for 3D or 4D, just means in 3D
    // not all the fields are defined.
    struct InterpolationStencil
    {
        int idx0[8];     // corners at tidx
        int idx1[8];     // corners at tidx_neighbor

        int tidx_neighbor;
        int xidx_neighbor;
        int yidx_neighbor;
        int zidx_neighbor;

        double t0;
        double frame_dt;

        double x0;
        double y0;
        double z0;

        double dx;
        double dy;
        double dz;
    };


    // Create and return a stencil that is used in interpolate_field to 
    // interpolate a 3D field
    __device__ __forceinline__
    InterpolationStencil build_stencil_3d(
        const Background::BackgroundDevice& bkg_d, int xidx, 
        int yidx, int zidx, const double x, const double y, const double z)
    {
        InterpolationStencil s;

        // Neighbor indices
        const int xidx_neighbor = Utilities::get_neighbor_index_cuda(
                x, d_x, xidx, bkg_d.xdim);

        const int yidx_neighbor = Utilities::get_neighbor_index_cuda(
                y, d_y, yidx, bkg_d.ydim);

        const int zidx_neighbor = Utilities::get_neighbor_index_cuda(
                z, d_z, zidx, bkg_d.zdim);

        s.xidx_neighbor = xidx_neighbor;
        s.yidx_neighbor = yidx_neighbor;
        s.zidx_neighbor = zidx_neighbor;

        // Indices at each vertex
        s.idx0[0] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim, 
            xidx, yidx, zidx);

        s.idx0[1] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            xidx, yidx, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx0[2] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            xidx, yidx_neighbor, zidx);

        s.idx0[3] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            xidx, yidx_neighbor, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx0[4] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            xidx_neighbor, yidx, zidx);

        s.idx0[5] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            xidx_neighbor, yidx, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx0[6] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            xidx_neighbor, yidx_neighbor, zidx);

        s.idx0[7] = Utilities::calc_3d_index_cuda(bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            xidx_neighbor, yidx_neighbor, zidx_neighbor);


        // x, y, z coordinates of two bounding vertices to interpolate 
        // between. Note these are not grid vertices, but rather are formed
        // by cell center coordinates since that's where the field is assumed
        // to be defined. It is essentially a cell shifted by dx/2, dy/2
        // and dz/2 if that helps.
        // d_x, d_y, d_z are from device_constants.cuh
        s.x0 = d_x[xidx];
        s.y0 = d_y[yidx];
        s.z0 = d_z[zidx];

        const double x1 = d_x[xidx_neighbor];
        const double y1 = d_y[yidx_neighbor];
        const double z1 = d_z[zidx_neighbor];

        s.dx = x1 - s.x0;
        s.dy = y1 - s.y0;
        s.dz = z1 - s.z0;

        return s;
    }


    // Create and return a stencil that is used in interpolate_field to 
    // interpolate a 4D field
    __device__ __forceinline__
    InterpolationStencil build_stencil_4d(
        const Background::BackgroundDevice& bkg_d, int tidx, int xidx, 
        int yidx, int zidx, const double x, const double y, const double z)
    {
        InterpolationStencil s;

        // Neighbor indices
        const int xidx_neighbor =
            Utilities::get_neighbor_index_cuda(x, d_x, xidx, bkg_d.xdim);

        const int yidx_neighbor =
            Utilities::get_neighbor_index_cuda(y, d_y, yidx, bkg_d.ydim);

        const int zidx_neighbor =
            Utilities::get_neighbor_index_cuda(z, d_z, zidx, bkg_d.zdim);

        // Time neighbor
        const int at_end = (tidx == static_cast<int>(bkg_d.tdim) - 1);
        const int tidx_neighbor = tidx + 1 - 2 * at_end;

        s.tidx_neighbor = tidx_neighbor;
        s.xidx_neighbor = xidx_neighbor;
        s.yidx_neighbor = yidx_neighbor;
        s.zidx_neighbor = zidx_neighbor;

        // Indices at t = tidx
        s.idx0[0] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx, yidx, zidx);

        s.idx0[1] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx, yidx, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx0[2] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx, yidx_neighbor, zidx);

        s.idx0[3] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx, yidx_neighbor, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx0[4] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx_neighbor, yidx, zidx);

        s.idx0[5] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx_neighbor, yidx, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx0[6] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx_neighbor, yidx_neighbor, zidx);

        s.idx0[7] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx, xidx_neighbor, yidx_neighbor, zidx_neighbor);

        // Indices at t = tidx_neighbor
        s.idx1[0] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx, yidx, zidx);

        s.idx1[1] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx, yidx, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx1[2] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx, yidx_neighbor, zidx);

        s.idx1[3] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx, yidx_neighbor, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx1[4] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx_neighbor, yidx, zidx);

        s.idx1[5] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx_neighbor, yidx, zidx_neighbor);

        s.idx1[6] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx_neighbor, yidx_neighbor, zidx);

        s.idx1[7] = Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda(
            bkg_d.xdim, bkg_d.ydim, bkg_d.zdim,
            tidx_neighbor, xidx_neighbor,
            yidx_neighbor, zidx_neighbor);

        // t, x, y, z coordinates of two bounding vertices to interpolate 
        // between. Note these are not grid vertices, but rather are formed
        // by cell center coordinates since that's where the field is assumed
        // to be defined. It is essentially a cell shifted by dx/2, dy/2
        // and dz/2 if that helps.
        // d_t, d_x, d_y, d_z are from device_constants.cuh
        s.t0 = d_t[tidx];
        const double t1 = d_t[tidx_neighbor];

        s.x0 = d_x[xidx];
        s.y0 = d_y[yidx];
        s.z0 = d_z[zidx];

        const double x1 = d_x[xidx_neighbor];
        const double y1 = d_y[yidx_neighbor];
        const double z1 = d_z[zidx_neighbor];

        s.dx = x1 - s.x0;
        s.dy = y1 - s.y0;
        s.dz = z1 - s.z0;

        s.frame_dt = t1 - s.t0;

        return s;
    }


    // Interpolate a 3D field at x,y,z. The stencil comes from build_stencil
    // above. 
    __device__ __forceinline__
    double interpolate_field_3d(const double* __restrict__ field,
        const InterpolationStencil& s, double x, double y, double z)
    {

        // Values at the 8 corners of the spatial interpolation stencil
        double verts0[8];

        // Calculate the 8 indices at tidx. 
        // pragma unroll just tells the compiler to break this loop 
        // down into 8 individual statements. This lets it use the 
        // register more efficiently and removes loop overhead.
        #pragma unroll
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i)
        {
            verts0[i] = field[s.idx0[i]];
        }

        // Trilinear interpolation within the spatial cell defined
        // by the stencil.
        return  Utilities::trilinear_interpolate(s.x0, s.y0, s.z0,
                s.dx, s.dy, s.dz, verts0[0], verts0[4], verts0[2], verts0[6],
                verts0[1], verts0[5], verts0[3], verts0[7], x, y, z);

    } // interpolate_field_3d


    // Interpolate a 4D field at t,x,y,z. The stencil comes from build_stencil
    // above. 
    __device__ __forceinline__
    double interpolate_field_4d(const double* __restrict__ field,
        const InterpolationStencil& s, double t, double x, double y, double z)
    {

        // Arrays to hold all 8 values at the vertices
        double verts0[8];
        double verts1[8];

        // Calculate the 8 indices at tidx and tidx_neighbor. 
        // pragma unroll just tells the compiler to break this loop 
        // down into 8x2 individual statements. This lets it use the 
        // register more efficiently and removes loop overhead.
        #pragma unroll
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i)
        {
            verts0[i] = field[s.idx0[i]];
            verts1[i] = field[s.idx1[i]];
        }

        // Trilinear interpolation at the particle location for this
        // field component, comp0, and then comp1 is the same just
        // at the next time index. I've lined the indices of v up with
        // the corresponding ones from the trilinear_interpolate 
        // signature.
        const double comp0 = Utilities::trilinear_interpolate(s.x0, s.y0, s.z0,
                s.dx, s.dy, s.dz, verts0[0], verts0[4], verts0[2], verts0[6],
                verts0[1], verts0[5], verts0[3], verts0[7], x, y, z);

        const double comp1 = Utilities::trilinear_interpolate(s.x0, s.y0, s.z0,
                s.dx, s.dy, s.dz, verts1[0], verts1[4], verts1[2], verts1[6],
                verts1[1], verts1[5], verts1[3], verts1[7], x, y, z);

        // Now linearly interpolate in time (this is just point slope)
        return comp0 + (comp1 - comp0) * ((t - s.t0) / s.frame_dt);

    } // interpolate_field_4d
}

#pragma once

#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>


namespace Utilities
{

    // Compute cross-product in-place, storing result in out
    __device__ __forceinline__ 
    void cross_product_cuda(const double a[3], const double b[3],
        double out[3])
    {
        out[0] = a[1] * b[2] - a[2] * b[1];
        out[1] = a[2] * b[0] - a[0] * b[2];
        out[2] = a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[0];
    }


    // Compute and return dot product
    __device__ __forceinline__ 
    double dot_product_cuda(const double a[3], const double b[3])
    {
        return a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[1] + a[2] * b[2];
    }


    // Find nearest neighbor index of val using cell_center as the locations
    __device__ inline 
    int get_neighbor_index_cuda(const double val,
        const double* cell_centers, int idx, int N)
    {
        // dx > 0 -> +1, dx < 0 -> -1
        double dx_from_center = val - cell_centers[idx];
        int side = 2 * (dx_from_center > 0.0) - 1;

        // Check grid edges
        int is_left_edge  = (idx == 0);
        int is_right_edge = (idx == N - 1);

        // Offset logic identical to CPU version
        int offset =
              side * (1 - is_left_edge - is_right_edge)
            + 1    * is_left_edge
            + (-1) * is_right_edge;

        return idx + offset;
    }

    // 4D -> 1D index for indexing Vector4Ds that are stored flattened
    __device__ inline 
    int calc_4d_index_cuda(int xdim, int ydim, 
        int zdim, int tidx, int xidx, int yidx, int zidx)
    {
        // This is from Vector4D::calc_index
        return tidx * (xdim * ydim * zdim) + xidx * (ydim * zdim) 
            + yidx * zdim + zidx;
    }

    // 3D -> 1D index for indexing Vector4Ds that are stored flattened
    __device__ inline 
    int calc_3d_index_cuda(int ydim, int zdim, int xidx, int yidx, int zidx)
    {
        // This is from Vector3D::calc_index
        return xidx * (ydim * zdim) + yidx * zdim + zidx;
    }


    // 1D linear interpolate for arrays that are known at compile time
    template <typename T, size_t N>
    __device__
    T linear_interpolate_cuda(const T (&xarr)[N], const T (&yarr)[N],
        T x)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < N - 1; i++)
        {
            if ((x >= xarr[i] && x <= xarr[i + 1]) ||
                (x <= xarr[i] && x >= xarr[i + 1]))
            {
                const T t = (x - xarr[i]) / (xarr[i + 1] - xarr[i]);
                return yarr[i] + t * (yarr[i + 1] - yarr[i]);
            }
        }

        // Should never happen for valid usage.
        return yarr[N - 1];
    }


    template <typename T>
    __device__ inline T bilinear_interp(const T* __restrict__ table,
        const T* __restrict__ x_grid, int nx, const T* __restrict__ y_grid, 
        int ny, T x, T y)                        
    {
        // --- 1. Find bracketing x indices ---
        int ix = 0;
        while (ix + 1 < nx && x_grid[ix + 1] < x)
            ix++;

        if (ix >= nx - 1)
            ix = nx - 2;

        T tx = (x - x_grid[ix]) /
                    (x_grid[ix + 1] - x_grid[ix]);

        // --- 2. Find bracketing y indices ---
        int iy = 0;
        while (iy + 1 < ny && y_grid[iy + 1] < y)
            iy++;

        if (iy >= ny - 1)
            iy = ny - 2;

        T ty = (y - y_grid[iy]) /
                    (y_grid[iy + 1] - y_grid[iy]);

        // Prevent extrapolation past edges
        tx = fmin((T)1, fmax((T)0, tx));
        ty = fmin((T)1, fmax((T)0, ty));

        // --- 3. Compute flattened indices ---
        int idx00 = ix * ny + iy;
        int idx10 = (ix + 1) * ny + iy;
        int idx01 = ix * ny + (iy + 1);
        int idx11 = (ix + 1) * ny + (iy + 1);

        T v00 = table[idx00];
        T v10 = table[idx10];
        T v01 = table[idx01];
        T v11 = table[idx11];

        // --- 4. Bilinear interpolation ---
        T vx0 = v00 + tx * (v10 - v00);
        T vx1 = v01 + tx * (v11 - v01);

        return vx0 + ty * (vx1 - vx0);
    }


    // Trilinearly interpolate the values defined by the 8 vertices at (x, y, z)
    __device__ inline 
    double trilinear_interpolate(
        const double x0, const double y0, const double z0, 
        const double dx, const double dy, const double dz,
        const double v000, const double v100, const double v010, 
        const double v110, const double v001, const double v101, 
        const double v011, const double v111,
        const double x, const double y, const double z)
    {
        // Normalized coordinates in [0,1]
        double tx = (x - x0) / dx;  // dx = x1 - x0
        double ty = (y - y0) / dy;
        double tz = (z - z0) / dz;

        // Prevent extrapolation beyond cell boundaries.
        tx = fmin(1.0, fmax(0.0, tx));
        ty = fmin(1.0, fmax(0.0, ty));
        tz = fmin(1.0, fmax(0.0, tz));

        // Interpolate along x for the four lower/upper face corners
        const double c00 = v000 + tx * (v100 - v000);
        const double c01 = v001 + tx * (v101 - v001);
        const double c10 = v010 + tx * (v110 - v010);
        const double c11 = v011 + tx * (v111 - v011);

        // Interpolate along y for the lower and upper edges
        const double c0 = c00 + ty * (c10 - c00);
        const double c1 = c01 + ty * (c11 - c01);

        // Interpolate along z and return
        return c0 + tz * (c1 - c0);
    }

docs.text:
Floating point type used in most of the simulation. 

using BkgFPType =  double;

This determines the precision used in the vectors within Background and Statistics classes. This is just to reduce memory overhead, since a Statistics object is copied for each thread, so the memory can balloon quickly. Only double and float are valid, but others could be added if there is a good reason.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <vector>


namespace Indices
{
    template <typename T>
    int get_nearest_index_cpu(const std::vector<T>& vec, const T value)
    {
        auto lower = std::lower_bound(vec.begin(), vec.end(), value);

        if (lower == vec.begin()) 
        {
            return 0;
        }
        if (lower == vec.end()) 
        {
            return vec.size() - 1;
        }

        auto prev = lower - 1;
        if (std::fabs(*lower - value) < std::fabs(*prev - value)) 
        {
            return lower - vec.begin();
        } 
        else 
        {
            return prev - vec.begin();
        }
    }


    template <typename T>
    int get_nearest_cell_index_cpu(const std::vector<T>& grid_edges, 
        const T value)
    {
        // Get the index of the first value in grid_edges that is larger
        // than value.
        auto lower = std::lower_bound(grid_edges.begin(), grid_edges.end(), 
            value);

        // Realize that one minus the index represented by lower is the value
        // we're after in the vectors with values at the cell centers.
        //  ____________
        //  |_0_|_1_|_2_|  <-- cell center indices
        //  0   1   2   3  <-- grid_edges indices
        //          ^
        //        lower
        //
        // In this example, we want 1 returned, so we return 2 - 1 = 1. If
        // value is outside the range, return the index of the respective end
        // of the vector.
        int index = std::distance(grid_edges.begin(), lower);

        // If less than everything, return the first cell.
        if (lower == grid_edges.begin()) return 0;

        // If larger than everything, return the last cell. Note end() is the
        // iterator that points past the last element of a vector, so to return
        // the cell we need to subtract by 2. 
        else if (lower == grid_edges.end()) 
        {
            return index - 2;
        }

        //else return lower - grid_edges.begin() - 1;
        else return index - 1;
    }

}  // namespace Indices

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

struct ParticleProgress 
{
    int tot_parts;
    int num_prints;
    int next_index;        // which checkpoint we are waiting for
    double step;           // percentage step per print (e.g., 10% if num_prints=10)

    ParticleProgress(int total, int prints)
        : tot_parts(total),
          num_prints(prints),
          next_index(1),
          step(100.0 / prints)
    {}

    // Call this whenever rem_parts changes
    void update(int rem_parts)
    {
        if (tot_parts <= 0 || num_prints <= 0) return;

        double pct_left = 100.0 * rem_parts / tot_parts;

        // Print while we've crossed one or more checkpoints
        while (pct_left <= 100.0 - next_index * step && next_index <= num_prints) 
        {
            std::cout << "Progress: " << std::lround(pct_left) 
                << "% remaining (" << rem_parts << " particles left)\n";
            next_index++;
        }
    }
};

#pragma once
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdint>

#include "constants.h"

// If using nvcc define this so that this struct can be used in CPU and GPU code
#ifdef __CUDACC__
#define HD __host__ __device__
#else
#define HD
#endif

// I just had AI give me this, very straightforward RNG that is STL-free and
// thus can be used in CUDA
struct pcg32 
{
    uint64_t state;
    uint64_t inc;

    bool has_spare {false};
    double spare {};

    HD
    pcg32(uint64_t seed, uint64_t seq) {
        state = 0;
        inc = (seq << 1u) | 1u;
        next_uint();
        state += seed;
        next_uint();
    }

    HD
    uint32_t next_uint() {
        uint64_t oldstate = state;
        state = oldstate * 6364136223846793005ULL + inc;
        uint32_t xorshifted = static_cast<uint32_t>(((oldstate >> 18u) ^ oldstate) >> 27u);
        uint32_t rot = static_cast<uint32_t>(oldstate >> 59u);
        return (xorshifted >> rot) | (xorshifted << ((-rot) & 31));
    }

    HD
    double next_double() {
        return (next_uint() >> 8) * (1.0 / 16777216.0);
    }

    // Box-Mueller transform for returning two normally distributed random
    // numbers centered on mean with standard deviation stddev. Since it
    // returns two numbers, we cache the second one to avoid throwing it away.
    HD
    double normal(double mean, double stddev)
    {
        // If spare random number was cached use it
        if (has_spare)
        {
            has_spare = false;
            return mean + stddev * spare;
        }

        // Box-Mueller transform for two normally distributed random numbers
        double u1 = next_double();
        if (u1 < 1e-12) u1 = 1e-12;

        double u2 = next_double();

        double r = sqrt(-2.0 * log(u1));
        double theta = 2.0 * Constants::pi * u2;

        // Cache the second number
        spare = r * sin(theta);
        has_spare = true;

        return mean + stddev * (r * cos(theta));
    }
};

#ifndef TIMER_H
#define TIMER_H

#include <array>
#include <chrono>
#include <string>

namespace Timer
{
    // One entry per code section you want to time. Add new sections here
    // only -- nothing else needs to change to support a new section.
    enum class Section : std::size_t
    {
        Total,
        Read,
        Imp,
        Boris,
        IonRec,
        Step,
        Coll,
        Bounds,
        FillSlots,
        FindCell,
        Record,
        AllDead,
        Save,
        Count  // sentinel -- must stay last, gives array size
    };

    // Per-section timing state. Each section owns its own start time and
    // "running" flag, so ending one section can never affect another.
    struct Accumulator
    {
        std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::time_point start{};
        double total_us {0.0};
        long long calls {0};
        bool running {false};
    };

    class Timer;

    // RAII scoped timer. Starts timing a section on construction and stops
    // it on destruction, so it can't be forgotten and is exception/early
    // return safe. Typical usage:
    //
    //   {
    //       ScopedTimer t(timer.acc(Section::Boris));
    //       push_boris(p);
    //   }
    //
    class ScopedTimer
    {
    public:
        explicit ScopedTimer(Accumulator& acc);
        ~ScopedTimer();

        // Not copyable or movable -- a scoped timer represents exactly one
        // live timing interval.
        ScopedTimer(const ScopedTimer&) = delete;
        ScopedTimer& operator=(const ScopedTimer&) = delete;
        ScopedTimer(ScopedTimer&&) = delete;
        ScopedTimer& operator=(ScopedTimer&&) = delete;

    private:
        Accumulator& m_acc;
    };

    class Timer
    {
    public:
        // Access the accumulator for a given section. Use with ScopedTimer,
        // or call start()/stop() on the returned reference's section
        // manually via the Timer methods below.
        Accumulator& acc(Section s);
        const Accumulator& acc(Section s) const;

        // Manual start/stop, for cases where RAII scoping isn't convenient.
        // Prefer ScopedTimer where possible.
        void start(Section s);
        void stop(Section s);

        // Merge another Timer's accumulators into this one (e.g. combining
        // per-thread or per-rank timers). Sums every field for every
        // section -- unlike a hand-picked operator+, adding a new Section
        // automatically gets merged correctly.
        void merge(const Timer& other);

        // Print a formatted summary of all sections to stdout.
        void print_summary() const;

        // Format a duration given in microseconds as a human readable
        // string, choosing the largest sensible unit.
        static std::string format_time(double time_us);

    private:
        static std::string string_precision(double value, int precision);
        static const char* section_name(Section s);

        std::array<Accumulator, static_cast<std::size_t>(Section::Count)> m_acc{};
    };
}

#endif

        const double z01, const double z11, const double x, const double y);


    // Trilinear interpolation at (x, y, z)
    double trilinear_interpolate(
        const double x0, const double y0, const double z0, 
        const double x1, const double y1, const double z1,
        const double v000, const double v100, const double v010,

    // Interpolate a Vector4D at (t0, x0, y0, z0)
    template <typename T>
    double interp_vec4d(const Vectors::Vector4D<T>& vec4d, 
        const std::vector<double> t, const std::vector<double> x,
        const std::vector<double> y, const std::vector<double> z,
        const double t0, const double x0, const double y0, const double z0);


    // Finds the indices of the two grid points that bracket a specified
    // coordinate value.
    std::pair<int, int> bracket_indices(const std::vector<double>& x, 
        double x0);


    // Broadcast vector from root rank to all other ranks
    template <typename T>
    void mpi_broadcast_vector(std::vector<T>& v, int root, MPI_Comm comm);


    template <typename T, std::size_t N>
    T linear_interpolate(const std::array<T, N>& xarr, 
        const std::array<T, N>& yarr, T x) 
        {

        // Check that arrays are of same size
        if (xarr.size() != yarr.size()) {
            throw std::invalid_argument("xarr and yarr must be of same size");
        }

        // Loop to find the interval
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N - 1; ++i) {
            if ((x >= xarr[i] && x <= xarr[i + 1]) 
                || (x <= xarr[i] && x >= xarr[i + 1])) {

                // Linear interpolation
                T t = (x - xarr[i]) / (xarr[i + 1] - xarr[i]);
                return yarr[i] + t * (yarr[i + 1] - yarr[i]);
            }
        }

        std::ostringstream err {};
        err << "x value is outside the interpolation range: " << x;
        throw std::out_of_range(err.str());
    }

}

#include <cuda_runtime.h> 

#include "background.h"
#include "background_device.h"

namespace Background
{

    // Copy background data to device, returning a BackgroundDevice object with
    // pointers to memory location on device.
    BackgroundDevice Background::to_device(int device_id)
    {
        BackgroundDevice bkg_d {};

    #ifdef USE_CUDA

        bkg_d.device_id = device_id;

        // In include/cuda/device_constants.cuh we define arrays like t, x, 
        // etc. in constant memory since they're small. Their size is set by
        // MAX_1D in that file. As time goes on this will need to be increased,
        // but for now print a error that if any dimension is above that you
        // WILL run into difficult to find errors due to accessing out of
        // bounds memory (which Nvidia GPUs don't care about).
        if (m_dim1 > MAX_1D || m_dim2 > MAX_1D
            || m_dim3 > MAX_1D || m_dim4 > MAX_1D)
        {
            std::cerr << "Error! MAX_1D is too small. It MUST be increased.\n"
                << "  dim1 = " << m_dim1 << "\n"
                << "  dim2 = " << m_dim2 << "\n"
                << "  dim3 = " << m_dim3 << "\n"
                << "  dim4 = " << m_dim4 << "\n";
        }

        bkg_d.tdim = m_dim1;
        bkg_d.xdim = m_dim2;
        bkg_d.ydim = m_dim3;
        bkg_d.zdim = m_dim4;

        int N_3D {m_dim2 * m_dim3 * m_dim4};
        int N_4D {m_dim1 * m_dim2 * m_dim3 * m_dim4};

        cudaSetDevice(device_id);

        // -----------------------------------
        // Constant memory copies
        // -----------------------------------

        // These arrays are great candidates for putting in GPU constant
        // memory since they are small. Arrays in constant memory can be read
        // significantly faster, which is convienent since these are read
        // very often. We declare them as constant in in 
        // cuda/device_constants.cuh, and use cudaMemcpyToSymbol to copy them 
        // into constant memory.
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_t, m_times.data(), m_dim1 * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_x, m_x.data(), m_dim2 * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_y, m_y.data(), m_dim3 * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_z, m_z.data(), m_dim4 * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_grid_x, m_grid_x.data(), (m_dim2+1) 
            * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_grid_y, m_grid_y.data(), (m_dim3+1) 
            * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_grid_z, m_grid_z.data(), (m_dim4+1) 
            * sizeof(double));

        double tmp[2];
        cudaMemcpyFromSymbol(tmp, d_x, 2*sizeof(double));

        // Copying scalars to constant memory is a little tricker since they
        // are not treated the same way as arrays. So we use this overload
        // of cudaMemcpyToSymbol which handles it.
        const double t_min {m_times.front()};
        const double t_max {m_times.back()};
        const double x_min {m_x.front()};
        const double x_max {m_x.back()};
        const double y_min {m_y.front()};
        const double y_max {m_y.back()};
        const double z_min {m_z.front()};
        const double z_max {m_z.back()};
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_t_min, &t_min, sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_t_max, &t_max, sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_x_min, &x_min, sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_x_max, &x_max, sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_y_min, &y_min, sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_y_max, &y_max, sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_z_min, &z_min, sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpyToSymbol(d_z_max, &z_max, sizeof(double));

        // -----------------------------------
        // Global memory allocation and copies
        // -----------------------------------

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dxdX, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dxdY, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dxdZ, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dxdX, m_dxdX.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dxdY, m_dxdY.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dxdZ, m_dxdZ.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dydX, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dydY, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dydZ, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dydX, m_dydX.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dydY, m_dydY.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dydZ, m_dydZ.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dzdX, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dzdY, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dzdZ, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dzdX, m_dzdX.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dzdY, m_dzdY.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dzdZ, m_dzdZ.get_data().data(), N_3D 
            * sizeof(double), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.ne, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.ne, m_ne.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.te, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.te, m_te.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.ti, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.ti, m_ti.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.bX, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.bX, m_bX.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.bY, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.bY, m_bY.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.bZ, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.bZ, m_bZ.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.bmag, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.bmag, m_bmag.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.eX, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.eX, m_eX.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.eY, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.eY, m_eY.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.eZ, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.eZ, m_eZ.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.emag, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.emag, m_emag.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.uX, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.uX, m_uX.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.uY, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.uY, m_uY.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.uZ, N_4D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.uZ, m_uZ.get_data().data(), N_4D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        // 3D arrays
        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dXdx, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dXdx, m_dXdx.get_data().data(), N_3D * sizeof(double),

            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dZdx, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dZdx, m_dZdx.get_data().data(), N_3D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dXdy, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dXdy, m_dXdy.get_data().data(), N_3D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dYdy, N_3D * sizeof(double));
        cudaMemcpy(bkg_d.dYdy, m_dYdy.get_data().data(), N_3D * sizeof(double), 
            cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

        cudaMalloc(&bkg_d.dZdy, N_3D * sizeof(double));

        return bkg_d;

#else
        std::cerr << "Error! Background::to_device() was called but GPU support"
                  << " was not compiled in.\n";
#endif
    }  // to_device

    {

        cudaFree(bkg_d.eX);      bkg_d.eX = nullptr;

        cudaFree(bkg_d.emag);    bkg_d.emag = nullptr;

        cudaFree(bkg_d.uX);      bkg_d.uX = nullptr;
